chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from some of our companions, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abu Maryam al-Ansari, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
Verily, the One who knows the number of the grains of sand in 'Alij (desert) surely knows that the obligatory shares (of inheritance) do not exceed six.

key_terms.الفرائض: The obligatory shares (fara'id): the fixed shares of inheritance specified in the Quran (4:11-12, 4:176)
key_terms.تعول: From 'awl: the doctrine whereby, when the sum of heirs' fixed shares exceeds the estate, each share is proportionally reduced. Shia jurisprudence rejects this.
key_terms.رمل عالج: 'Alij desert sands: a proverbial expression of an immense, uncountable number, used to underscore divine omniscience

ai.seo_question: Does the Shia school of law accept the doctrine of 'awl (proportional reduction) in inheritance?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) invokes divine omniscience — using the vast number of sand grains in the 'Alij desert as a rhetorical measure of certainty — to establish the jurisprudential principle that the Quranic inheritance shares (fara'id) cannot exceed a total of six primary fractions. This is a direct refutation of the doctrine of 'awl (proportional reduction of shares when they exceed the estate), which was accepted by some Sunni jurists. The Imam's argument is that since God, who knows all things, legislated these shares, they are perfectly balanced and require no adjustment.
